title: Retreat from moderation shifts information risk toward users and under-resourced local trust networks
source_unit: Northwestern University Roberta Buffett Institute and Center for Communication & Public Policy, Global Disinformation in a Post-Moderation World synthesis report, published 10 September 2026
geography: Global information ecosystems, with examples from the United States, Taiwan, Ukraine, and Spanish-language communities

institutional_retreat.value: The report describes platforms reducing moderation and governments reducing counter-disinformation programs, shifting more responsibility to journalists, civil society, communities, and individual users

accountability_gap.value: The central governance question becomes who bears information risk when amplification, recommendation, and monetization remain powerful but safeguards retreat

post_moderation.value: A post-moderation information environment need not become a post-accountability environment, but accountability has to be redistributed across platforms, regulators, journalism, civil society, and users

observations.method: Northwestern-led symposium synthesis drawing on panels with researchers, journalists, platform and civil-society practitioners, and public-policy experts; this is not a probability sample or representative public-opinion survey.
observations.uncertainty: The publication summarizes expert claims and examples rather than estimating global exposure, causal effects, or the comparative performance of moderation interventions.
observations.subgroup: Platform users, journalists, civil-society organizations, public institutions, local experts, and communities with different language and information-access conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Retreat from a prior moderation model may reflect legitimate concerns about speed, ambiguity, and protected expression; alternative accountability arrangements could improve pluralism if they are transparent and contestable.

observations.period: September 2026; trust collapse and social coordination

trust_erosion.value: The report treats the deeper danger as loss of confidence in information, institutions, journalism, elections, and the possibility of determining truth, rather than belief in one false claim alone

coordination_route.value: Confusion, distrust, polarization, and paralysis can impair a society's ability to think, coordinate, and act coherently

epistemic_retreat.value: Citizens may disengage or retreat into trusted political and social communities when they no longer know which information can be trusted

observations.method: Expert synthesis of political-communication, disinformation, and information-resilience discussions in the symposium report.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not measure the prevalence of generalized distrust or establish that any particular campaign caused disengagement, enclave formation, or institutional failure.
observations.subgroup: Citizens, voters, news audiences, public decision-makers, and communities exposed to polarized or adversarial information flows.
observations.counterinterpretation: Skepticism can sometimes improve scrutiny and pluralism; distrust of one source does not necessarily imply distrust of all information or political withdrawal.

observations.period: September 2026; distribution, attention, and local trust

denominator.unit: symposium synthesis of intervention and distribution cases

attention_problem.value: People may care about truth but fail to consider accuracy while scrolling and sharing emotionally engaging content

trusted_distribution.value: Accurate information is insufficient when it does not reach communities through trusted local media, grassroots groups, interpersonal networks, or culturally legible messengers

local_capacity_gap.value: Local organizations often hold the most relevant cultural and linguistic knowledge while having the least sustained staffing, technical, and communications capacity

observations.method: Symposium synthesis drawing on discussion of Spanish-language journalism, community organizations, local expertise, accuracy prompts, and trusted-messenger interventions.
observations.uncertainty: The report provides illustrative cases and expert interpretation, not a comparative evaluation of reach, cost, effectiveness, or durability across channels.
observations.subgroup: Language minorities, local journalists, community organizations, creators, fact-checkers, and users whose information access depends on trusted intermediaries.
observations.counterinterpretation: Local trust networks can also narrow exposure, reproduce exclusion, or carry inaccurate claims; proximity and cultural fluency are not guarantees of accuracy or inclusion.

observations.period: September 2026; AI-enabled influence and information infrastructure

denominator.unit: symposium synthesis of AI and state-sponsored-disinformation cases

dual_use_ai.value: AI can support personalized corrections, rapid question answering, and narrative monitoring while also making deepfakes, synthetic personas, scams, and tailored influence operations cheaper and more scalable

adversarial_goal.value: State-sponsored campaigns may seek to make elections and institutions appear untrustworthy and to polarize rather than persuade citizens toward one stable narrative

infrastructure_response.value: The proposed response shifts from isolated fact-checking toward provenance, quality signals, escalation procedures, auditability, platform transparency, local expertise, and shared responsibility

observations.method: Symposium synthesis of examples involving Taiwan, Ukraine, Spanish-language information distribution, AI-assisted interventions, and platform accountability.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not quantify the scale or success of the cited campaigns and does not show that the proposed infrastructure would reduce political violence, polarization, or institutional distrust.
observations.subgroup: Voters, language communities, journalists, public institutions, platforms, civil society, and populations targeted by state or commercial influence operations.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI-supported verification and personalization may improve access and resilience, but provenance and transparency systems can be politicized, costly, or used to over-restrict legitimate speech.

related_sources.claim: Northwestern Center for Communication & Public Policy provides institutional context for the symposium.
Chicago Council on Global Affairs was identified as a symposium partner.

boundary: This record adds an information-governance route from platform and government retreat through attention, trust, local distribution capacity, AI-enabled influence, provenance, and public coordination. It is a symposium synthesis and expert interpretation, not a representative survey, causal evaluation, exposure estimate, or proof that any proposed accountability arrangement will work.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Northwestern publication page reviewed for the post-moderation framing, trust and coordination mechanisms, distribution and local-capacity examples, AI dual-use, state-sponsored influence, and infrastructure/accountability proposals.
